title: The sun for breakfast
hookLine: baby Hanuman leaps for the sun and comes home with every god's gift; why Hindus ask him for courage

lines: THE SUN LOOKS LIKE A MANGO.
cards: A baby wakes up hungry. His mother is off gathering fruit. Low on the horizon he sees the rising sun, round and orange-red, exactly like a ripe mango.
So he jumps for it. Not a hop: this baby is the son of the wind, and he shoots straight up into the sky, mouth open, reaching for breakfast. The gods watch in alarm.
And Indra, king of the gods, lord of storms, does what a nervous king does. He throws his thunderbolt. It strikes the baby on the jaw, and he falls all the way to earth.

teach.b: The baby is Hanuman, and the fall gives him his name. Hanu means jaw in Sanskrit. Hanuman: the one with the jaw, the one who was struck.
The story is in the Ramayana, the great epic credited to the poet Valmiki, where an old bear, Jambavan, tells it to Hanuman himself. Some tellings say a fruit; many families say a mango.
Then comes a shape you've met before.
Hanuman's father is Vayu, the wind. When his son falls, Vayu carries him into a cave and stops blowing. The whole world begins to suffocate.

teach.h: EVERY GOD GIVES HIM A GIFT.
teach.b: They heal the child, and each one gives him a gift: strength, speed, protection from weapons, a long life. Even Indra gives one. The baby knocked out of the sky goes home carrying the gifts of every god.

teach.h: WHY HINDUS PRAY TO HANUMAN FOR STRENGTH.
teach.b: This is why Hindus pray to Hanuman for strength and protection. He isn't only a hero in a story; he's worshipped as a god, with temples of his own, and many devotees visit them on Tuesdays or Saturdays.
In Hindi he's often called Bajrangbali, the mighty one with a body like the thunderbolt.

Asking Hanuman for courage is asking for strength the gods themselves put in him. Some families keep a small Hanuman in the car for just that reason. And notice: the tradition doesn't mock the baby for reaching too high.
It names him for that very day.

how: Hanuman is one of the most widely worshipped figures in Hinduism; many Hindus visit his temples on Tuesdays or Saturdays, and his childhood stories are told to children as the start of his life.

o: the son of Indra, named for the storms his father rules
the one with the jaw, named for where the thunderbolt struck
the one who flies, from an old Sanskrit word for wind

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.

s: Hanuman's name comes from where the thunderbolt hit him
hanu means jaw: the one who was struck on the jaw.
the gods punish Hanuman for reaching for the sun
they heal him, and each gives him a gift.
Hindus worship Hanuman as a god, not only as a hero in a story
he has temples of his own, and devotees ask him for strength and protection.

games.q: you're Vayu, the wind. your baby son has been struck out of the sky. what do you do?
o: forgive Indra and carry on blowing.
take your son into a cave and stop.
blow a storm against Indra's palace.
games.why: he stops, and the whole world can't breathe. the gods come, heal the child, and give him gifts.

practice: Settle, and breathe slowly, like the wind coming back. Bring to mind something ahead of you that scares you a little: a test, a hard talk, a first day.

If you pray, say softly a few times, Om Hanumate Namah, a bow to Hanuman, and ask for his courage. If you don't, picture that baby knocked out of the sky and sent home full of gifts, and let your fear sit beside that picture.

wordCard.voice: Hanuman. The one with the jaw, named for the thunderbolt that struck him as he leapt for the sun.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the one with the (marked) jaw, from hanu, jaw.

carryVoice: Your line: Hanuman holds every god's gift. That's why Hindus ask him for courage. Tomorrow, the strength he forgot he ever had. That's day twenty-nine.
